The test image shows a corn ear with husks pulled back, revealing yellow kernels with patches of grayish-green mold scattered across the ear. The tip appears dark/damaged. This is a seed/ear disease.

Top candidates from seed/pod classes: Trichoderma_Ear_Rot, Aspergillus_Ear_Rot, Fusarium_Disease, Diplodia_Ear_Rot, Gibberella_Disease, Common_Smut.

Let me view reference images one at a time, starting with my top candidates.
Trichoderma reference shows dark blue-green/black mold on kernels. The test image mold appears lighter/more grayish-green. Let me check other candidates.
Aspergillus shows heavy olive-green powdery mold covering large areas. The test image has more scattered grayish patches, less powdery. Let me check Fusarium.
Fusarium shows whitish-pink mold, not matching the grayish-green in the test image. Let me check Diplodia.
Diplodia shows grayish-brown mummified kernels viewed from the cob cross-section. Very different from the test image. Let me check Gibberella.
Gibberella shows pinkish-white mold at the tip. Not matching. Let me revisit Trichoderma with another reference, and also check the pod image.
Let me check another Aspergillus reference for comparison.
This Aspergillus reference matches the test image well: olive-green to grayish mold patches on kernels with damaged tip. Let me use my last view to check one more reference.

This confirms it. The test image shows a corn ear with olive-green to gray-green powdery/moldy patches on and between kernels, with the tip darkened and damaged. This matches Aspergillus Ear Rot closely: the olive-green powdery mold on kernels, damage concentrated toward the tip, and scattered patches across the ear. The Trichoderma references showed darker blue-green/black mold, while Fusarium was whitish-pink and Gibberella was pinkish-red. The color and distribution pattern in the test image aligns best with Aspergillus.
